anti_police_summary: Amazon imposed a one-year moratorium on police use of Rekognition facial recognition on June 10, 2020 during the George Floyd protests, then extended it indefinitely in May 2021; in 2024 it also removed Ring's 'Request for Assistance' feature that had let police request doorbell-camera footage without warrants.

Nike made Colin Kaepernick the face of its 30th-anniversary 'Just Do It' campaign in September 2018 (an explicit endorsement of his anti-police-brutality protest), then in June 2020 pledged $40M (Nike/Converse/Jordan) plus a separate $100M from Jordan Brand/Michael Jordan over 10 years to racial-justice and criminal-justice organizations, with 2023 grantees including NAACP LDF, ArchCity Defenders (which files civil-rights suits against police) and Citizens for Juvenile Justice.

Apple launched its Racial Equity and Justice Initiative (REJI) on June 11, 2020 after the police killing of George Floyd, initially committing $100M and doubling it to over $200M by June 2023, with funds flowing to criminal-justice reform groups including the Anti-Recidivism Coalition; CEO Tim Cook also published an open 'Speaking up on racism' letter explicitly tying the program to Floyd's killing by Minneapolis police.

On June 8, 2020, CEO Arvind Krishna sent a letter to Congress announcing IBM would no longer offer general-purpose facial recognition or analysis software and opposed its use by police for mass surveillance and racial profiling; IBM further divested its i2 law-enforcement analytics portfolio (Analyst's Notebook, iBase) to N. Harris Computer Corporation effective January 1, 2022.

Microsoft President Brad Smith announced on June 11, 2020 that the company would not sell facial-recognition technology to US police departments until a federal law regulating it is in place; the ban was reinforced and extended on May 2, 2024 when Microsoft updated Azure OpenAI Service terms to explicitly prohibit use of generative AI for facial recognition by US police and globally for real-time FR on body-worn/dash cameras.

In December 2018, SVP Kent Walker announced Google would not sell general-purpose facial recognition APIs until 'important technology and policy questions' were resolved; Google also published 2018 AI Principles banning weapons and surveillance applications, declined to renew the Project Maven defense contract, has given multi-million-dollar Google.org grants for criminal-justice reform (e.g., $8M expansion announced 2020, including Code for America record-clearance work), and in December 2023 changed Location History storage to client-side, effectively undermining police geofence warrants.

In June 2020 CEO Bob Chapek and Executive Chairman Bob Iger condemned the police killing of George Floyd and Disney pledged $5 million to social-justice nonprofits, starting with a $2 million donation to the NAACP, but with no concrete change to Disney's own law-enforcement relationships.

In 2018 JPMorgan Chase 'banned the box' on job applications and later launched the Chase PolicyCenter and a Second Chance Agenda committing ~$7M to remove employment barriers for people with criminal records; CEO Jamie Dimon publicly said 'justice was served' after the Derek Chauvin conviction (April 2021), and a small portion of the firm's $30B 2020 Racial Equity Commitment was directed to criminal-justice-reform organizations.

In June 2020 CEO Mark Zuckerberg pledged $10M from Facebook/Meta to 'groups working on racial justice' in response to George Floyd protests and calls to end police violence, and in November 2021 Meta shut down Facebook's facial-recognition system and deleted more than 1 billion face templates as part of a company-wide retreat from FR — a market the rest of Big Tech had exited over police-misuse concerns.

Unilever subsidiary Ben & Jerry's published an explicit 'Defund the Police' statement and petition on Juneteenth 2020, calling US policing 'racist and ineffective' and demanding it be 'dismantled' — the statement and petition page remain live on benjerry.com as of 2025.

On May 31, 2020, CEO Chip Bergh announced a $100,000 grant to the ACLU for criminal justice reform and racial justice work, plus a $100,000 grant to Live Free (Pastor Mike McBride) following George Floyd's killing.

In June 2020, DoorDash committed $1 million to racial-justice causes, including a $500,000 donation directly to Black Lives Matter (whose platform centrally calls for defunding police) plus another $500,000 directed by its Black Employee Resource Group.

In June 2020, CEO Dara Khosrowshahi announced Uber would donate $1 million split between the Equal Justice Initiative and the Center for Policing Equity (which measures racial bias in policing) as part of a broader $10M+ 'anti-racist' pledge.

In June 2020 Lululemon donated $100,000 to the Minnesota Freedom Fund (cash-bail abolition group) and pledged $250,000 across organizations including Black Lives Matter (which advocates defunding police) and local Minneapolis groups, in response to George Floyd's killing.

In June 2020 Airbnb donated $500,000 split between the NAACP and the Black Lives Matter Foundation (matching employee donations to both), and later added a $100,000 contribution to the NAACP Legal Defense and Education Fund — groups that advocate for police accountability and have been associated with the 'defund' movement.

In June 2020 WarnerMedia (the predecessor merged into WBD in April 2022) donated commercial ad inventory to Color of Change and the NAACP Legal Defense Fund — both criminal-justice/police-reform groups — and in October 2020 Warner Bros. Television Group signed an overall production deal with BLM co-founder and 'defund the police' advocate Patrisse Cullors, which quietly expired in October 2022 with no shows produced.

In June 2020 following George Floyd's killing, then-president Dave Kimbell announced Ulta would donate (undisclosed amount) to the Equal Justice Initiative to 'support... efforts to challenge racial and economic injustices,' alongside expanded diversity training.

As part of a $530M racial-justice commitment announced June 11, 2020 after George Floyd's murder, PayPal pledged $500,000 to the Equal Justice Initiative (criminal-justice reform) and $500,000 to Borealis Philanthropy's Black-Led Movement Fund, alongside CEO Dan Schulman's repeated public commitments to racial justice through 2021.

In June 2020, Netflix pledged $5M to Black creator/youth organizations including a $1M grant to Colin Kaepernick's Know Your Rights Camp (a police/criminal-justice reform-adjacent group), and CEO Reed Hastings personally donated $1M to the Center for Policing Equity.

Chubb's Rule of Law Fund began in 2020 funding racial-justice/police-reform grants and in May 2021 awarded $1.1M, including $350,000 to the Policing Project at NYU Law School and $250,000 to the Vera Institute of Justice's Motion for Justice, with renewed grants announced March 21, 2023 to groups working on police-community relations (e.g., Equal Justice USA's Trauma to Trust in Newark).

In July 2020 Salesforce pledged $200M over five years for racial equality and justice and publicly advocated for 20+ state/federal criminal-justice and police-reform bills covering data transparency and accountability.

In Dec 2018 Google Cloud (Kent Walker) publicly declined to offer general-purpose facial recognition APIs pending policy work, and in June 2020 after George Floyd's murder Alphabet/Google.org committed ~$12M to racial-equity groups plus ~$6M in criminal-justice-reform grants including $1M each to the Movement for Black Lives and the Center for Policing Equity.

In June 2020 ELC committed $10M over three years to racial equity, with employee-matched donations directed to Black Lives Matter Global Network Foundation, Equal Justice Initiative, NAACP Legal Defense and Educational Fund, and Race Forward — groups working on criminal justice and policing reform.

On June 8, 2020 Comcast/NBCUniversal CEO Brian Roberts announced a $100M multiyear plan ($75M cash + $25M media) for social justice that named the Equal Justice Initiative, NAACP Legal Defense Fund, National Urban League, NAACP and National Action Network as grantees — organizations that litigate and advocate around police misconduct and criminal-justice reform.

In June 2020, following the George Floyd protests, EA CEO Andrew Wilson committed $1 million in corporate donations to the Equal Justice Initiative, the NAACP Legal Defense & Educational Fund, and other racial-justice/criminal-justice organizations, plus a 2-for-1 employee match.

Launched the $10M Goldman Sachs Fund for Racial Equity on June 3, 2020, naming 'Legal & Criminal Justice Reform' as one of four pillars and funding grantees including the NAACP Legal Defense and Educational Fund, in response to the killings of George Floyd, Breonna Taylor and Ahmaud Arbery.

On Aug 5, 2020, Prudential announced expanded racial equity commitments including accelerating its public policy agenda on 'criminal justice reform, police reforms addressing racism,' with the Prudential Foundation funding partnerships on criminal justice and police reform as part of its $1B+ giving portfolio.

Following George Floyd's killing, Qualcomm/Qualcomm Charitable Foundation launched a $500,000 racial justice initiative (2020) directing grants to criminal-justice and police-reform-adjacent groups including the Equal Justice Initiative, ACLU Foundation, and Lawyers' Committee for Civil Rights Under Law.

In June 2020 Capital One pledged $10M to social-justice organizations for Black communities and subsequently funded the Congressional Black Caucus Foundation's National Racial Equity Initiative for Social Justice (NREI), which explicitly addresses criminal justice reform 'through the policy lens of... incarceration, the courts and law enforcement.'

In June 2020, Yum! Brands (KFC, Pizza Hut, Taco Bell, Habit Burger) pledged $3 million to the NAACP Legal Defense and Educational Fund, the ACLU, and Louisville-based social-justice nonprofits following the police killings of George Floyd and Louisville-resident Breonna Taylor, later expanded to a $100M Unlocking Opportunity Initiative and $6M for Louisville.
